kin.draftText: He gave up a war band to become a monk, and soon began “to long for the wilderness”. He spent the rest of his life as a hermit on an island in the fens. His Life says there was “so much cheerfulness in him, that he always appeared alike to acquaintances and to strangers.”
kin.concerns: Both halves are strong and recorded as his settled nature: cheerful (the Life's closing portrait, plus 'cheerful in mood' as a young monk and 'with cheerful countenance and good humour' with visitors), and quiet (he longed for the wilderness and lived as a hermit at Crowland for about 15 years, until he died). Caveats: (1) Before his conversion he led a war band for about nine years ('It was about nine years that he was thus engaged in hostile raids'), which is the restless opposite; the card handles it honestly in its first sentence. (2) The quotations come from the Old English translation of Felix's Latin Life (c. 740), in Goodwin's 1848 English. I could not check Felix's Latin, because Colgrave's 1956 edition is lending-only on archive.org. The Old English words ('wynsum on his mode', 'glaednys' = gladness) carry the same sense. Goodwin's line breaks 'acquaint-ances' and 'wilder-ness' across lines; the words are 'acquaintances' and 'wilderness'. I cross-checked every quotation against a second scan (archive.org anglosaxonversi00goodgoog). (3) Visitors kept coming to him (bishops, nobles, the exiled king Athelbald), and he received them warmly, so he was a hermit but not a recluse. A tidbit for a saint page: two visiting monks hid their ale bottles under a turf on the way; he asked them 'with merry countenance and laughing words' why they had not brought them along. He is in the Roman Martyrology (11 April). Files: scratchpad kin/hearth-early/guthlac_clean.txt and guthlac2.txt.

verdict.reasons:
I tried to refute him and could not. He is a fair fit for the Hearth. The card needs one change (see below).

CHEERFUL HALF. The source records it as his settled nature at every stage of his life, not as a single moment:
- as a child: "blithe in countenance" (ch. II, p. 13; Old English "glaed on his ansyne")
- as a young monk: "cheerful in mood"
- with visitors: "with cheerful countenance and good humour", and he "received it smiling" (ch. XI, p. 57)
- teasing the two monks about their hidden ale: "with merry countenance and laughing words" (ch. XV, p. 65)
- in the closing portrait (ch. XX, p. 93)
Felix's Latin, which I checked in Gonser's 1909 edition, backs this up:
- "hilari facie" (cheerful face) for the boy
- "hilari vultu ... nam semper gratia eximiae charitatis in ore ipsius et vultu fulgebat" ("always") at the glove scene
- "hilari vultu leviter subridens ludibri famine" (a cheerful face, a slight smile, joking words) at the ale scene
So this is a lifelong temper and a real sense of humour. It is not only holy joy.

QUIET HALF. This is strong from the age of 26. He longed for "the wilderness and a hermitage". The fen was "his beloved wilderness", and "he was enamoured of the obscurity of the place". He stayed there "serving God for fifteen years" until he died. He was also "mild and modest in his discourse". The caveat has to be said: from about 15 to 24 he led a war band ("It was about nine years that he was thus engaged in hostile raids"). The source also says his longing for solitude came after he heard about the old hermits and was "inspired with the love of God". So the quiet is recorded as a love and a vocation he took up as an adult, not as his nature from youth. The site accepted Antony on the same kind of evidence, and the card names the war band openly, so I judge it fair. He also welcomed many visitors, which matches the Hearth's "a long talk".

MAIN PROBLEM, which I have fixed. The closing portrait is a stock passage. Felix copied it almost word for word from Sulpicius Severus on St Martin. Felix's Latin reads: "Nemo vidit illum iratum ... nullus moerentem: sed unus idemque semper permanens laetitiam in vultu ... ita ut extra humanam naturam notis ignotisque esse videretur". Martin's Oak card on this site already quotes the same passage: "he was always one and the same". The draft card's "he always appeared alike to acquaintances and to strangers" is that same passage, rewritten by the Old English translator; the Latin says he seemed "beyond human nature" to people who knew him and people who did not. With it, the site would use one borrowed passage to prove confident steadiness for Martin and cheerfulness for Guthlac, and a careful reader could catch that. The fixed card drops that clause. It keeps "evermore sweetness was in his temper" and leads with the ale story, which comes from Felix's own local material.

SMALLER FIXES. "Soon" became "two years later" in the concerns, and the card now says he led the war band. The card has no section numbers and no pronouns for God.

PICTURE. Public-domain portraits exist. On Wikimedia Commons, "File:Guthlac-Contemplation-BL.jpg" (913x906) and "File:Guthlac-Bartholemew.png" (3400x3060) are both tagged Public domain (Guthlac Roll, British Library Harley Roll Y 6, c. 1210). The G.F. Storm etching (Wellcome V0032177) is tagged CC BY 4.0 on Commons, not PD, so it needs a credit line.

He is in the Roman Martyrology on 11 April.

verdict.quoteProblems:
None of the seven quotations is missing or altered. Each one is word for word in Goodwin 1848, which is public domain. The only breaks in the printed text are line-end hyphens: "wilder-ness" and "acquaint-ances". The chapter and page citations are correct: ch. II p. 19, ch. III p. 23, ch. XV p. 65 and ch. XX p. 93.

Two notes on the source. (1) The closing line "there was so much cheerfulness in him, that he always appeared alike to acquaintances and to strangers" is the Old English translator's reworking. Felix's Latin says he seemed "beyond human nature" to people who knew him and people who did not. That Latin was itself copied from Sulpicius Severus's portrait of St Martin, whom the site already uses (the Oak) with the line "he was always one and the same". For that reason the card should not rest on this clause. (2) All the English quotations come from the Old English version, not from Felix's Latin, so the source line should say so.

Two phrases in the concerns were also verified word for word: "with cheerful countenance and good humour" and "It was about nine years that he was thus engaged in hostile raids". Other exact lines that are useful for a saint page: "blithe in countenance" (ch. II p. 13), "he was enamoured of the obscurity of the place" (ch. III p. 23), "received it smiling" (ch. XI p. 57) and "serving God for fifteen years" (ch. XX).
verdict.fixedText: He led a war band for nine years, then became a monk and began “to long for the wilderness”. He spent his last fifteen years as a hermit on an island in the fens. His Life says “evermore sweetness was in his temper”. When two visiting monks hid their ale under a turf on the way, he knew. He asked them “with merry countenance and laughing words” why they had not brought it along.

kin.draftText: He came from Syria to Spoleto in Italy. When the town offered him houses and money, he walked out and “built a little cottage for himself” in a lonely place. St Gregory says his one fault was that “sometime he would so exceed in mirth, that if men had not known him to have been so full of virtue, none would ever have thought it.”
kin.concerns: The cheerful half is strong and recorded as a lasting trait: Gregory names his mirth as the one thing in him that seemed blameworthy. He then explains that God leaves small faults in great people to keep them humble. The quiet half is clear but not strong. He chose a cottage in a lonely place over the town's offers, but disciples soon gathered and he governed them as their abbot ('A monk that seeketh for livings upon earth is no monk'). This is the strongest tie-in available to the test itself. The test's own author describes a holy man with the cheerful temper and its exact trap: results.mjs quotes Gregory's 'pleasure borders on mirth' as the cheerful trap. So one card shows both the gift and the fault. He is little known, which is weak for search. The 1608 English keeps old forms ('sometime', 'strook'); quote it exactly. He is in the Roman Martyrology (11 April: 'whose virtues are remembered by pope saint Gregory the Great', per Italian Wikipedia). File: scratchpad kin/hearth-early/greg_dial_3.txt.

verdict.who: St Isaac of Spoleto (Isaac of Monteluco), 6th century, a Syrian hermit and abbot near Spoleto, remembered in the Roman Martyrology on 11 April
verdict.reasons:
QUOTES. I fetched https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_03_dialogues_book3.htm again myself. It is the P.W. 1608 translation as edited by Gardner in 1911, so it is public domain. All three quotations match it word for word: the mirth line, "But the servant of almighty God ... built a little cottage for himself" and "And so he began his devotions ... likewise the night following." I also checked the Latin (la.wikisource, Dialogi Liber III caput XIV). It reads "quod nonnunquam tanta ei laetitia inerat, ut ... nullo modo crederetur", which means "not seldom there was such gladness in him that..."

CHEERFUL HALF: recorded and strong. This was a trait, not one moment. Peter asks whether he loosened "the reins of gladness" on purpose or whether his mind was drawn to joy "even resisting". Gregory answers that God leaves small faults in people He gives great gifts, so they stay humble. That treats the mirth as a lasting part of his character. It is also exactly the cheerful trap in results.mjs ("pleasure borders on mirth"), described by the test's own author, which makes this a strong fit.

QUIET HALF: only partly recorded. Gregory never says Isaac loved quiet or found busy days hard, which is how the test defines a quiet mind (MAKEUPS.quiet). The evidence is his way of life. First, he prayed three days and nights without tiring. That shows devotion, and it was not "alone" as the candidate's note says. It happened in a public church, and a keeper accused him of praying "in the sight of the world". The candidate's note should be corrected. Second, he left the crowds who wanted to take him home and built a hut in a desert place, where he lived until he died. Gregory gives poverty as the reason ("so fearful he was to lose the secure state of his poverty"), not a love of quiet. Disciples then gathered and he governed them as abbot. His mirth could suit a Spark as easily as a Hearth, and nothing in the source settles which. So he meets the site's current bar about as well as Arsenius ("fled the world to pray") and Benedict's cave years do. He is weaker than Antony, whose withdrawals Athanasius explains as flight from the crowds. Mark him `partial: true`. If the card must say it, one honest line would be: "His love of quiet shows in how he lived more than in anything Gregory says of him."

DRAFT CARD FIXES. (1) "offered him houses" is not quite right. People tried to take him home to their own houses, and they offered land and money. (2) It left out Gregory's own explanation of the fault. A fair reader, and a reverent one, needs it, or the card reads as a saint being mocked. (3) It was slightly long and repeated "mirth". The fixed text keeps the quotation exact, including the archaic "sometime" (Latin nonnunquam, meaning "at times"). It uses a capital He for God and shows no chapter numbers. The source line has no chapter numbers either.

OTHER. He is canonized: Italian Wikipedia says the Roman Martyrology remembers him on 11 April. He is little known, which is weak for search.

PORTRAIT: no public-domain portrait found. The Commons images of his crypt under Sant'Ansano in Spoleto are CC BY-SA, not public domain. 'Santisacco z02.jpg' (CC BY-SA 2.5) shows the sarcophagus, not a face. A Commons category "Sant'Ansano (Spoleto) - Frescos" (11th- to 12th-century crypt frescoes) exists. Commons blocked further requests (rate limit) before I could check whether any of them shows Isaac, and photos there usually carry a CC licence. The card needs an illustration or no portrait.
verdict.quoteProblems: None in the quotations. All three are word for word at the URL, and the translation is public domain (1608, edited 1911). One error in the candidate's note: it says the three days of prayer were "alone in the church". The source says the opposite. He prayed in public, and a keeper called him a hypocrite for praying "in the sight of the world" (Latin: "ante oculos hominum"). Do not use that as evidence of solitude.
verdict.fixedText: He came from Syria to Spoleto in Italy. The town offered him land and money. He refused it all and “built a little cottage for himself” in a lonely place. St Gregory says he had one fault: “sometime he would so exceed in mirth, that if men had not known him to have been so full of virtue, none would ever have thought it.” God often leaves a small fault in people He has given great gifts, Gregory explains, so they do not grow proud.

kin.draftText: For years he longed for “the secrecy of solitude”, and at last he lived alone on the island of Farne. Bede says he spoke to people “with cheerful and soothing language, as he was accustomed”. They pulled him off the island in tears to make him a bishop, and within two years he went back to “his much-loved solitude”.
kin.concerns: The quiet half is strong: he long wanted solitude, lived as a hermit on Farne, was dragged off it 'with tears in his eyes' to be bishop, and went back to it to die. The cheerful half is clear but mild. Bede records a habit of cheerful, gentle talk. His verse Life (Latin checked at intratext.com/X/LAT0423.htm) says 'ut erat placidus' and 'ore iucundus' (pleasant of speech), which reads as gentle and pleasant more than merry. As a boy he loved 'mirth and clamour', but gave up 'vain sports' after a child rebuked him. There is counter-evidence for the quiet mind. He was a tireless walking preacher before Farne, and he said being woken pleased him because 'by rousing me from inactivity, he enables me to do or think of something useful'. So he is partial, but famous, which is strong for search. A Hearth tidbit for a saint page (ch. 27): brothers visiting him on Farne for Christmas asked to 'spend a joyful day'. He agreed, and during the 'eating, merriment, and conversation' he twice warned them to stay watchful. That is Gregory's cheerful trap in miniature. Giles's translation is 19th-century, public domain. File: scratchpad kin/hearth-early/bede_cuthbert.txt.

verdict.who: St Cuthbert of Lindisfarne (c. 634-687), for the Hearth (cheerful + quiet)
verdict.quoteProblems:
I fetched https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/bede-cuthbert.asp again (Giles, 19th century, public domain) and checked all six quotations. Each one appears word for word. My copy is at scratchpad/skeptic_cuthbert/bc.txt.
- One chapter number is wrong. "he divested himself of his episcopal duties and returned to his much-loved solitude" opens CHAPTER XXXVI in this translation, not ch. 37. Cite ch. 36.
- The other five are in the chapters given: ch. 11, 19, 1, 17 and 24.
- Giles softens Bede's Latin in two places. I checked the Latin in Stevenson's 1841 Opera historica minora (public domain): https://archive.org/download/venerabilisbeda00bedegoog/venerabilisbeda00bedegoog_djvu.txt.
  - In ch. 11, "as he was accustomed" translates "ut jocundus atque affabilis erat", which means "cheerful and affable as he was".
  - In ch. 19, "in a cheerful and affable manner" translates "quia laeti vultus et affabilis erat", which means "because he had a glad face and was affable".
  - Both changes weaken the evidence. Nothing in the English overstates the Latin.
- A stronger line about his nature, checked word for word in the same Giles text at ch. 7: "He was affable and pleasant in his character". The Latin is "affabilis et jocundus moribus erat".
- The Christmas story in the concerns needs one fix. In ch. 27 he warns the brothers three times, not twice. They only listen after the third warning. Also, it is the brothers who ask to "spend a joyful day". Cuthbert is the watchful one in that story, not the one who gives in.
verdict.reasons:
Both halves hold up, and the cheerful half is stronger than the drafter thought.

CHEERFUL: Bede presents it as his character, not one moment.
- Ch. 7: "He was affable and pleasant in his character" (Latin: affabilis et jocundus moribus erat).
- Ch. 11: "cheerful and soothing language, as he was accustomed" (Latin: ut jocundus atque affabilis erat).
- Ch. 19: "he used, in a cheerful and affable manner" (Latin: laeti vultus et affabilis erat).
- Ch. 1: as a boy he "took delight ... in mirth and clamour".
That runs from boyhood to old age, so it reads as temper, not grace in one scene. Ch. 16 adds that he kept a steady face through hardship. There Giles says "placidity of countenance" where the Latin says faciem hilarem, a cheerful face. The drafter judged it "gentle more than merry" from the verse Life. The prose Latin word jocundus is closer to cheerful.

QUIET: strongly recorded, partly in his own words.
- Ch. 17: "the secrecy of solitude which he had so long coveted".
- Ch. 24: "send me back to my former solitude and quiet" (his own words).
- Ch. 24: many messengers failed to bring him in, so the king sailed to Farne. They drew him off "with tears in his eyes".
- Ch. 36: after two years as bishop he went back to "his much-loved solitude".
The quiz already names Gregory the Great and Gregory the Theologian for the quiet mind on this same pattern: they loved quiet and had the busy life forced on them.

WHAT COUNTS AGAINST HIM, and it should be said. He was energetic.
- Ch. 1: as a boy he was "agile by nature", the one who held out when the others were tired.
- Ch. 9: in his Melrose years he walked for weeks to preach in remote villages.
- Ch. 16: he said being woken pleased him, because "by rousing me from inactivity, he enables me to do or think of something useful".
- Ch. 11: in the storm, his cheerful words themselves are "Why do we remain here idle?"
That is close to Gregory's restless marker. But it shows he disliked idleness, not busy crowds. What he asked for, again and again, was solitude and quiet.

Would a fair reader agree? Yes. Cuthbert is widely remembered as the gentle, pleasant hermit of Farne. With the counterweight noted, he is a sound second Hearth. He would sit beside Antony.

PICTURE: public-domain options exist on Wikimedia Commons.
- File:Athelstan.jpg: the frontispiece of CCCC MS 183, c. 930, tagged public domain, 1330x2000. It shows King Athelstan presenting a book to Cuthbert.
- Category "Life of St. Cuthbert (late 12th C) - BL Yates Thompson MS 26": manuscript miniatures that may give a better face crop. I could not check their licence tags because Commons returned HTTP 429.
- A photo of a Dublin Christ Church stained-glass Cuthbert, tagged public domain.

CARD FIXES:
- It now opens with the nature statement.
- It keeps "as he was accustomed" in its storm scene, told in plain words.
- It says the king himself fetched him, which is accurate to ch. 24. The draft said "they pulled him off", which was vaguer.
- "Within two years" becomes "after two years", which matches Bede's "When Cuthbert had passed two years".
- Every sentence is short. There are no section numbers and no pronouns for God.
verdict.fixedText: Bede says he was “affable and pleasant in his character”. Once a storm stranded him and some brothers without food. He still spoke to them “with cheerful and soothing language, as he was accustomed”. He had long wanted “the secrecy of solitude”, and at last he lived alone on the island of Farne. When he was chosen as a bishop, the king himself sailed out to fetch him. After two years he went back to “his much-loved solitude”.

kin.concerns: The quiet half is the stronger and plainest (solitude "so long coveted", "much-loved", "solitude and quiet" in his own words, dragged from Farne in tears). The cheerful half is recorded as character and habit ("in his character", "as he was accustomed") but in fewer, milder words than More's. Bede also shows him tireless: preaching rounds, whole nights of prayer, walking round Lindisfarne at night, and his saying that being woken gives him pleasure "by rousing me from inactivity" (ch. 16). So do not paint him as idle; the card does not. One Farne Christmas story (ch. 27) shows him warning the brothers against too much merriment at a feast; harmless, but a reader of the full Life will see a grave side too. verdict.fixedText: Bede says he was “affable and pleasant in his character”. He liked to tell people, “in a cheerful and affable manner”, what God had done for him. But he had long wanted to live alone, and at last he went to the island of Farne. Made a bishop against his will, he gave it up after two years. Then he went back to “his much-loved solitude”.

verdict.quoteProblems:
None of the quotations is missing or altered. I fetched https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/bede-cuthbert.asp again myself (HTTP 200) and searched the stripped text for each one. All nine match Giles word for word. That covers the seven listed plus "although much resisting, he was overcome by the unanimous wish of all" and "rousing me from inactivity". The chapter numbers are right too: 7, 11, 19, 17, 24, 24, 36 and 16. The translation is J. A. Giles, first published 1843 and reprinted in Everyman 479 in 1910. It is public domain.

Two notes on the translation, neither of them a defect:
(a) In ch. 11, Giles's "as he was accustomed" is a loose rendering. The Latin (la.wikisource, Vita prosaica S. Cuthberti, from Migne PL 94) reads "ut jocundus atque affabilis erat", which means "as he was cheerful and affable". So the source states it as his nature, which is stronger than habit.
(b) In ch. 19, the Latin behind "in a cheerful and affable manner" is "solebat enim saepe, quia laeti vultus et affabilis erat", meaning "because he had a glad face and was affable". "Laetus" is the very word Gregory uses for the cheerful in Pastoral Rule III.3 ("laeti" and "tristes").

Ambiguity check: "drew him away from his retirement with tears in his eyes" is ambiguous in Giles's English. The Latin settles it: "ipsum quoque lacrymis plenum dulcibus extrahunt latebris". The tears are Cuthbert's own, and they drew him from his "sweet" retreat. My working copies are saved in the scratchpad at skeptic-cuthbert/bede.txt and lat.txt.
verdict.reasons:
I tried to refute this candidate and could not. The source is close to the man. Bede wrote around 721, from the Lindisfarne anonymous Life of about 700 and from Herefrith, who was with Cuthbert when he died.

CHEERFUL: yes, recorded as nature, not one moment. Ch. 7 says "affable and pleasant in his character" (Latin: "affabilis et jucundus moribus", cheerful in his ways). Ch. 11 says "as he was accustomed" (Latin: "as he was cheerful and affable"). Ch. 19 says he "used" to talk "in a cheerful and affable manner" (Latin: "laeti vultus", a glad face, Gregory's own word). Ch. 16's Latin also has him keeping "faciem hilarem", a cheerful face, even amid troubles; Giles softens this to "placidity of countenance". That is four notes of temper at the level of character or habit. The English words are milder than the Latin, but a fair reader would still agree.

QUIET: yes, and this is the stronger half. He "so long coveted" solitude (ch. 17). In his own words he looked for "solitude and quiet" (ch. 24). He could not be moved from Farne by letters or messengers. The king had to sail out and kneel, and Cuthbert left in tears, "much resisting" (ch. 24). After two years as bishop he went back to "his much-loved solitude" (ch. 36). Ch. 37 gives "about two months in the enjoyment of his rest"; the Latin is "in magna repetitae suae quietis exsultatione".

Rating: quiet strongly, cheerful clearly. This should be stated as "one half strongly, the other clearly".

Caveats a reader of the full Life will see. None of them breaks the fit:
(1) He was tireless. He went on preaching tours in the hills of up to a month (ch. 9). He walked round the island at night. He said being woken pleased him "by rousing me from inactivity" (ch. 16). This is zeal against sloth, not a restless mind that goes bad when idle.
(2) As a boy under eight he "took delight ... in mirth and clamour" and was "agile by nature" (ch. 1). That is Spark-like, but Bede says he laid it aside as a man.
(3) At a Christmas feast on Farne he warned the brothers against too much merriment (ch. 27), so he had a grave side too.

He is not on the taken list and does not appear anywhere in the repo, so there is no duplicate.

Draft card: its sentences are plain and short, and the one capital it needs (God) is there. I changed three things.
- "Visitors still came, and he told them..." tied the cheerful manner to Farne visitors in particular. Bede says only that he "used" to tell "his hearers", so the fix says "He liked to tell people".
- I dropped the archaic "secrecy of solitude".
- I split the last sentence in two.

kin.concerns: The cheerful half is the strongest record of anyone I checked: a close friend says merriment "seems to be part of his nature". The quiet half is clear but it is his nature and wish, not his outward life. He was one of the busiest men in England (lawyer, Speaker, Lord Chancellor), and Erasmus adds in the same breath: "though he enjoys ease, no one is more alert or patient when duty requires it". Say it that way (like Gregory the Great's card: loved quiet, had the busy life forced on him); never call him a recluse. The Hearth portrait's "a meal, a long talk, an evening at home" fits him closely: Erasmus says talk with friends is "the principal charm of life" to him, and his house was full of pet birds and animals. His famous prison jokes are joy in suffering, so they are left out as evidence. Western saint, canonized 1935; the sources themselves are public domain. verdict.reasons:
I downloaded both texts again myself from archive.org: Bridgett 1891 (lifewritingsofs00brid_djvu.txt) and Roper, 1905 Burns & Gates edition (lifeofsirthomasm00ropeuoft_djvu.txt). Both are public domain. I checked all 11 quotations word for word, including the "though he enjoys ease..." clause from the concerns. Every one is present and unaltered once the OCR line-break hyphens are joined. None comes from a copyrighted translation.

CHEERFUL HALF, strongly recorded as his nature by two close witnesses. Erasmus, a friend of 20 years who stayed in his house, says merriment "seems to be part of his nature". He adds that More's face was "always expressive of an amiable joyousness". The candidate missed a second witness: Roper, his son-in-law, who lived in the house. Roper says "he was of a pleasant disposition". He also calls More's mirth "his nature": More "began thereupon somewhat to dissemble his nature, and so, by little and little, from his former mirth to disuse himself". So this is a settled temper, not one moment. As the candidate says, the prison jokes are rightly left out.

QUIET HALF: clear, but weaker than the candidate claims. It is recorded as his nature and his wish, not as his outward life.
(a) Erasmus says "By nature More is chary of his liberty and of ease". But the same sentence goes on: "no one is more alert or patient when duty requires it". That is the opposite of Gregory's quiet mind, which "give[s] way at the very beginning" when business comes.
(b) The court quotation is weaker evidence than it looks. Erasmus gives the reason for More's dislike of court as "a great hatred of constraint (tyrannis) and loves equality". That is love of freedom, not of quiet. Bridgett also frames it as unwillingness to take honours.
(c) Roper's "to be solitary" was "for godly purposes", a habit of prayer. It is holiness more than temperament, so it is only supporting evidence.
(d) The draft's "At home he built" is slightly wrong. Roper says the New Building was "a good distance from his mansion-house".
(e) Against the quiet half: Erasmus calls him "born and framed for friendship", "easy of access to all" and "full of jokes and banter". His house was full of visitors and animals. There is no "few words" at all.

STRONGEST QUIET EVIDENCE, which the candidate missed. Roper tells how the king and queen delighted in More's talk. They called for him at supper so often that he "could not once in a month get leave to go home to his wife and his children (whose company he most desired)". So he hid his merry nature until they sent for him less. One true episode from a close source records both halves. It puts home over court, which matches the Hearth line "an evening at home", and he is not made a recluse. Roper also says he lived "about four years" at the London Charterhouse "without vow", which backs the wish for quiet.

A fair reader who knows More as a busy statesman would accept the Hearth if the card says it this way: light by nature, loved home and ease, and the busy life was pressed on him (compare Gregory the Great's Deep Well card). I rewrote the draft around the Roper episode. It uses plain short sentences, has no section numbers and has no pronouns for God. Both quoted pieces were re-checked against the fetched texts.

Other notes. He is 16th century, so this goes against the preference for the first millennium, but that is a preference, not a rule. He was canonized in 1935. PORTRAIT: the Commons file page for Holbein's 1527 portrait (Frick) was fetched and shows "Public domain". Suggested slug: thomas-more. Mark him as a clear, not strong, fit on the mind half.
verdict.quoteProblems:
No quotation is missing or altered, and all come from public-domain texts. Problems of use:
(1) "No one ever strove more eagerly to gain admission there than More did to avoid it" is not in Bridgett's full translation of the letter. Bridgett quotes it on another page as from the Hutten letter. Erasmus gives the reason as hatred of constraint and love of equality, so it proves love of freedom more than love of quiet.
(2) "By nature More is chary of his liberty and of ease" continues in the same sentence with "yet, though he enjoys ease, no one is more alert or patient when duty requires it". Quote the second half too, or do not lean on the first alone.
(3) Roper's "sometimes to be solitary" is "for godly purposes": it describes devotion, not temper.
(4) The draft's "At home he built" contradicts Roper, who says the building was "a good distance from his mansion-house".
(5) The Tower quotation's "straight" means strait (narrow), as the candidate says. Do not show it to readers unexplained.
(6) The OCR splits "ad- mission" across a line; the words are correct once joined.
verdict.fixedText: His friend Erasmus wrote that since boyhood “he has so delighted in merriment, that it seems to be part of his nature.” The king and queen loved his talk and kept calling for him at supper. Soon he could not get home even once a month to his wife and children, “whose company he most desired”. So he slowly hid his merry side at court, and they sent for him less.

verdict.who: St Guthlac of Crowland (c. 674-714), for the Hearth
verdict.reasons:
I re-fetched Goodwin's 1848 translation myself (archive.org anglosaxonversio00guthrich_djvu.txt; archive.org metadata says NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, dated 1848). All six quotations appear there word for word. I also checked Felix's Latin through Gonser 1909 (archive.org Gonser_Das_angelsachsische_djvu.txt), which prints the Latin beside the Old English. I used it only for checking.

CHEERFUL, recorded as a habit, not one moment. Five separate places in the Life show it:
(a) In childhood he was "blithe in countenance". The Latin is "hilari facie".
(b) At Repton he was "cheerful in mood". This one is weak (see quoteProblems).
(c) He went out to three visitors "with cheerful countenance and good humour" and took the glove "smiling". The Latin adds "semper": grace always shone in his face.
(d) He teased two monks who had hidden their ale, "with merry countenance and laughing words". The Latin is "hilari vultu leviter subridens ludibri famine".
(e) The closing portrait says "so much cheerfulness in him, that he always appeared alike to acquaintances and to strangers". Felix's Latin is stronger still: nobody ever saw him sad ("nullus moerentem"), and he was "semper permanens laetitiam in vultu".
Several episodes and a summary saying "always" meet the standard. A fair reader would agree.

QUIET, recorded. He "began to long for the wilderness and a hermitage", began "to dwell alone among the fenny thickets", "was enamoured of the obscurity of the place", went back to "his beloved wilderness", and stayed there fifteen years until he died. The Life frames the move as a call from God after reading about the anchorites. The same is true of Antony, the Hearth's current kindred, and "beloved" and "enamoured" record a personal love of the hidden place. The restless half is his youth: about nine years of raiding, and the Latin says a love of ruling burned in him. The card says this openly, which the standard requires.

CAVEATS, none fatal:
1. The closing portrait is modelled on Sulpicius Severus's portrait of St Martin (Life of Martin 27). The site already quotes that passage for Martin on the Oak card ("he was always one and the same"). I checked the NPNF English at newadvent.org/fathers/3501.htm. Felix adapted it rather than copying it: he dropped Sulpicius's "nor laughing" and added "to known and unknown". The episodes in (c) and (d) are specific to Guthlac, so the claim does not rest on the borrowed lines.
2. The card attributes the words to Felix, but they come from the Old English version.
3. The Hearth's "a meal, an evening at home" fits a man who ate barley bread once a day poorly. The fit is about temper.

PORTRAIT: File:Guthlac-Contemplation-BL.jpg exists on Commons. It is the Guthlac Roll, British Library, c. 1210, marked Public Domain Mark, PD-old-100-expired and PD-Art. It is a roundel, not a face.

CARD FIXES in fixedText:
- "for nine years" becomes "for about nine years".
- "lived alone ... until he died" is replaced. Beccel the priest lived with him and was there at his death, and he came to Crowland with two servants.
- "cheerful in mood" is swapped for the ale-bottles line, which the Latin supports and which is a good tidbit.
- The long closing quotation is trimmed, and the rest is paraphrased in plain words.
- No pronouns for God, no section numbers.
verdict.quoteProblems:
No quotation is missing or altered. All six match Goodwin 1848 word for word. Only OCR artefacts differ: "acquaint- ances" across a line break, "weut" for "went", "bhthe" for "blithe".

Substantive problems:
(1) "cheerful in mood" is Goodwin's English for the Old English "wynsum on his mode" ("pleasant/winsome in his mind"). At this point Felix's Latin reads "mente devotus" ("devout in mind"). So the word "cheerful" here comes from the Old English translator, not from Felix. Do not open the card with it or call it Felix's word. I have replaced it.
(2) "so much cheerfulness in him ... always appeared alike to acquaintances and to strangers" is accurate to both the Old English ("swa mycel glaednys"; the manuscript reads "glaednysse", so there is no emendation, checked on the page image of p. 92) and the Latin ("laetitiam in vultu ... notis ignotisque"). But Felix modelled the passage on Sulpicius's portrait of St Martin, whom the Oak card already uses. It is a hagiographic topos adapted to Guthlac, not a free-standing observation. Keep it as the summary, not the only proof.
(3) The draft's "for nine years" should be "about nine years" ("It was about nine years that he was thus engaged in hostile raids").
(4) The draft's "He lived alone in the fens at Crowland until he died" overstates. He arrived "with two servants", and "a brother with him whose name was Beccel" was with him at his death.
(5) The candidate's chapter labels ("ch. 3", "ch. 4") follow no printed numbering that I could confirm. The closing portrait does sit at the end of Goodwin's ch. XX, and the ale story is ch. XV, "Concerning the brothers who came to him". None of this shows on the card.
verdict.fixedText: He led a war band for about nine years, then became a monk. He soon “began to long for the wilderness and a hermitage”. He lived as a hermit in the fens at Crowland for fifteen years. Once two visiting monks hid their ale under a turf. He asked them, “with merry countenance and laughing words”, why they had not brought it in. Felix, who wrote his Life, says “there was so much cheerfulness in him” that friends and strangers always found him the same.
verdict.fixedSrc: Felix, Life of St Guthlac (Old English version)

verdict.quoteProblems:
I fetched every source myself. All three English quotations match Reeves's 1874 translation word for word, and that translation is public domain.
(1) The "beloved by all ... holy joy ever beaming on his face" line: the uoft scan the candidate cites garbles "holy joy" as "h°ty j°7". A second scan of the same 1874 book reads "holy joy" cleanly (line 9931): https://archive.org/download/bub_gb_8VULAAAAYAAJ/bub_gb_8VULAAAAYAAJ_djvu.txt. Cite that URL for the Second Preface quotations.
(2) "He never could spend the space of even one hour..." and "So incessantly was he engaged..." are exact in both scans.
(3) The Psalter passage from his last evening is exact on the Fordham page. Fordham reprints Reeves 1874, and the candidate's chapter number (Book III, ch. 23) is right. The Fordham page does NOT include the Second Preface, so quotations (1) and (2) can only be cited to archive.org.
(4) A small error in the candidate's Latin: the scan reads "laetificabatur", not "laetificatus". The full sentence is "Et inter haec omnibus carus, hilarem semper faciem ostendens sanctam, Spiritus Sancti gaudio intimis laetificabatur praecordiis." "hilarem semper" (always cheerful) is confirmed. One manuscript (F) leaves out a word at that point, and D reads "semper hilarem".
The draft card's phrase "for the love of Christ" is also exact in Reeves.
verdict.reasons:
CHEERFUL: passes. Adomnan records it as a lasting habit, not one moment: "hilarem semper faciem", an always-cheerful face. He sets it beside "omnibus carus", dear to all. This matches what the Hearth already accepted for Antony (Athanasius: a cheerful face from a soul at peace). Two cautions. Adomnan credits the joy to the Holy Spirit. And the sentence is a stock saint's-life line (next paragraph).

RESTLESS: weaker than the "strong" the candidate claims. The whole case rests on "He never could spend the space of even one hour without study, or prayer, or writing, or some other holy occupation." I compared the Latin. Adomnan adapted this sentence from Sulpicius Severus's Life of St Martin 26.3: "numquam hora ulla momentumque praeteriit, quo non aut orationi incumberet aut insisteret lectioni". Adomnan's version is "Nullum etiam unius horae intervallum transire poterat, quo non aut orationi aut lectioni vel scriptioni vel etiam alicui operationi incumberet". The cheerful-face line likewise echoes Martin 27.1 ("unus idemque fuit semper, caelestem quodammodo laetitiam vultu praeferens"). The same Life, in Roberts's New Advent translation, says of Martin: "Never did a single hour or moment pass in which he was not either actually engaged in prayer" and "displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance". Reeves's own 1874 introduction notes that Adomnan quotes Sulpicius's Life of Martin. This site already files Martin under the Oak, which is QUIET, using that very chapter. So the formula alone records constant devotion, not a restless mind. The activities it names are prayer, reading and copying, the quietest kinds of work. Adomnan also shows Columba often going off alone to pray: "a place more remote from men and fitting for prayer"; "Today I wish to go alone to the western plain"; on Skye he "went alone a little farther than usual to pray". The fasting-and-vigils quotation records hardship, not a restless mind. The Psalter quotation is one deed on one evening. It makes a good closing detail but is not evidence. The restless reading gets real support only from Adomnan's additions to Sulpicius, "writing, or some other work" and "could not" let an hour pass. His busy life as a missionary and founder of monasteries cannot count, because a temper may not be inferred from deeds. So the restless half is present but not strong. Mark the card `partial`.

A FAIR READER: most readers would find a cheerful, never-idle missionary abbot a believable Spark. Two things may draw objections. Later Irish legend, not Adomnan, gives him a hot temper and blames him for the battle of Cul Dreimne. And in Book II Adomnan's own Columba curses plunderers. Keep the card to Adomnan's words, as the draft does. Adomnan wrote about a hundred years after Columba died. He was abbot of Iona and a kinsman, and he says he drew on earlier written records, so the source is close enough.

CARD: I cut "Yet". In the Latin the contrast is with the hardships, not with constant work, so it read oddly after a sentence about work. I quote "beloved by all" word for word, and I added the true last-evening detail in plain words. No section numbers. There are no pronouns for God in the text, and "Holy Spirit" is capitalised.

verdict.who: St Willibrord (c. 658-739), apostle of the Frisians. Candidate for The Spark (cheerful + restless).
verdict.reasons:
I tried to refute it and could not. Both halves are recorded as settled traits in the same early Life. The draft card needed rewriting, though, because it put Alban Butler's paraphrase in quotation marks as if it were Alcuin's words.

WHAT THE SOURCE RECORDS. In chapter 24, Alcuin gives a portrait of Willibrord's lasting qualities. Wattenbach's Latin (about p. 58) reads: "omni dignitate praeclarus, statura decens, vultu honorabilis, facie venustus, corde laetus, consilio sapiens, ore iucundus, moribus compositus, in omni opere Dei strenuus". Alexander Grieve's 1923 translation (p. 120) gives it as "cheerful in spirit, wise in counsel, pleasing in speech, sedate in character, and strenuous in all divine work".
- The cheerful half is a trait of his nature in a list of permanent traits. It is not one happy moment.
- The restless half is recorded several times over: "His love shows itself in the unremitting labours that he bore daily for the name of Christ". He "made progress in the divine work every day of his life". "In whose love he never ceased to work as long as he lived among us" (p. 121). He was "friendly to all people", and he went on from Frisia to the Danes, Heligoland and Walcheren.
- A fair reader would accept "cheerful and tireless" as a Spark.

LIMITS TO STATE HONESTLY:
(a) The cheerful evidence is thin. It is two adjectives, corde laetus and ore iucundus, in a eulogy that Grieve himself calls one "who will see no spots in the sun".
(b) Alcuin never knew him. Alcuin was born about 735 and Willibrord died in 739. Alcuin wrote about 796, from an older Life that is now lost. So the card must not say Alcuin "remembers" him.
(c) The restless half is recorded as untiring work. Nothing says stillness was hard for him. Alcuin also calls him "sedate in character" (moribus compositus), and the verse Life calls him "paciens, moderatus". So he was calm in manner and tireless in work. The card must not claim he could not sit still.
(d) Twelve years of study in Ireland and a retirement in old age do not count against his temper.
Fit: good, not "strong".

PORTRAIT. Commons API confirms File:Georg_Sturm,_Willibrordus_predikt_het_Christendom_aan_de_Friezen.jpg is tagged "Public domain", credited to the Rijksmuseum (5220x4952). It is a preaching scene, not a face, so it would need cropping, or a medieval Echternach miniature could be used instead.

A BETTER TRANSLATION WAS MISSED. The candidate thought the only public-domain English was Butler's and set aside Talbot (1954). But there is a direct, plainly public-domain translation of Alcuin: Alexander Grieve, "Willibrord, Missionary in the Netherlands, 691-739, including a translation of the Vita Willibrordi by Alcuin of York" (SPG, 1923). It was published in 1923, so it is public domain in the US, and Grieve died in 1952, so it is public domain in the UK too. PDF: https://medievalchurch.org.uk/pdf/e-books/grieve_alexander/willibrord_grieve.pdf (ch. 24 on p. 120, "never ceased to work" on p. 121). Talbot is not needed. The card's quotations now come from Grieve, and each one was checked word for word in that PDF.

1. "always cheerful in his speech and countenance": word for word in Butler, 1812 scan, vol. 11 p. 150. The OCR garbles "countenance", but EWTN's transcription of Butler confirms it. It is Butler's paraphrase, not a translation. "Always" has no basis in the Latin (there is no semper), and "cheerful in his speech and countenance" merges facie venustus, corde laetus and ore iucundus. The draft card puts these words in quotation marks as what Alcuin "remembers", which misattributes them. Replaced with Grieve's direct translation.

8. Factual slip in the draft: "He left England to preach to the Frisians". He had spent twelve years in Ireland and sailed from there (Alcuin 4-5; Bede V.10).

verdict.who: St Cuthbert of Lindisfarne (c. 634-687), put forward as a Spark. I recommend moving him to the Hearth instead.
verdict.quoteProblems:
None of the quotations is missing or altered. I re-fetched https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/bede-cuthbert.asp (saved as scratchpad/skeptic-cuthbert/bede.txt). All eight quotations appear word for word. The chapters are right: 7, 11, 19, 1, 1, 16, 16 and 9. The translation is J. A. Giles (1843), reprinted in Everyman's Library 479 (Dent, 1910). It is public domain.

I also checked Bede's Latin on Wikisource (Vita prosaica S. Cuthberti). In places Giles changes the strength of what Bede says:
(a) Ch. 11. Giles has "as he was accustomed". The Latin is "ut jocundus atque affabilis erat", which means "as he was cheerful and affable". This makes the cheerful half stronger.
(b) Ch. 19. The Latin is "quia laeti vultus et affabilis erat", "because he had a glad face and was affable". Also stronger.
(c) Ch. 16. Giles has "placidity of countenance". The Latin is "faciem praetendens hilarem", "showing a cheerful face" when sad things happened.
(d) Ch. 16. Giles has "relieved the tediousness of psalmody". The Latin "longitudinem" means only "length". Giles is reading in the restlessness.
(e) Ch. 16. Giles has "rousing me from inactivity". The Latin is "discusso torpore somni", "shaking off the heaviness of sleep". So the saying is about being woken for vigil, not about hating a quiet life. This makes the restless reading weaker.

The draft card says "He even thanked anyone who woke him". Bede does not say he thanked anyone. He says being woken pleased him, and he scolded the brothers who minded it.
verdict.reasons:
REJECT AS A SPARK. HE IS A STRONG HEARTH CANDIDATE.

THE CHEERFUL HALF IS SOLID. Bede records it three times as his character, not as one moment. Ch. 7: "affabilis et jucundus moribus erat", in Giles "He was affable and pleasant in his character". Ch. 11: "ut jocundus atque affabilis erat". Ch. 19: "laeti vultus et affabilis erat". Ch. 16 adds a cheerful face in hard times. Ch. 34 records him answering "jocose", as a joke. A fair reader would agree he had a cheerful temper.

THE RESTLESS HALF DOES NOT HOLD UP. What supports it:
- As a boy he was "agile by nature" (ch. 1). But the same chapter says that as a man he "most abundantly laid aside all those childish things". It also says God sent a child "to curb the sallies of his youthful mind". Leading the card with his boyhood games goes against what Bede says.
- His month-long preaching journeys (ch. 9) were part of his job as prior, "as Boisil, his predecessor, had done before him".
- Refusing to be idle (ch. 11) and working with his hands through night vigils (ch. 16) are the usual monk's watchfulness. The Latin of the saying about being woken is about the heaviness of sleep (see quoteProblems).

Against it, Bede records the quiet half more often and more strongly, as what Cuthbert wanted:
- Ch. 1 opens the whole Life with this: he "rejoiced to sit apart for no small space of time, and for the sweetness of divine meditation to hold his tongue silent from human colloquy".
- Ch. 17: "the secrecy of solitude which he had so long coveted". Bede says he rejoiced to go up from the active life "ad otium divinae speculationis" ("to the leisure of divine contemplation"). This is Gregory's own active and contemplative pattern, and Bede puts him on the quiet side.
- Ch. 18: he shut himself in his cell. He talked to visitors only through a window, then closed that too.
- Ch. 22: "despising secular cares, he preferred to live apart".
- Ch. 24, his own words: "send me back to my former solitude and quiet". The queen tells him "thou preferrest the recesses of thy desert to this rank".
- Ch. 36: after two years as bishop he "returned to his much-loved solitude".

The Spark portrait says "A quiet week makes you restless". Bede says the opposite of him. Gregory's restless mind gets only "worse labour" when work stops. Bede says Cuthbert rejoiced in contemplative quiet. Readers who know him as the hermit of Farne would object, with the text on their side. The drafter's own note already flags this.

AS A HEARTH HE FITS BY THE SAME TEST THAT PUT MARTIN OF TOURS IN THE OAK:
- A cheerful temper recorded as his nature.
- A love of solitude recorded again and again.
- A hermit who still talked with the brothers who came to visit (ch. 36: "he was accustomed to go out frequently from his cell, and converse with the brethren").

One caveat must be said on the card: he was never idle. He built his own cell and a guesthouse and grew barley (ch. 17 and 19). Gregory's "quiet" mind is one that gives way under business, and he handled priorship and bishopric well. So call him "partial" there too. The fixedText below is a HEARTH card, NOT a Spark card. Every quotation in it is verbatim in Giles and checked.

IF THE MAIN SESSION KEEPS HIM AS A SPARK ANYWAY, the draft must be fixed:
- Drop the boyhood lead.
- Replace "thanked anyone who woke him" with what Bede says: waking him gave him pleasure.
- Add a sentence about the solitude.
- Mark him partial.
For example: "Bede says he was “affable and pleasant in his character”. He told the brothers that being woken pleased him: “by rousing me from inactivity, he enables me to do or think of something useful.” He loved solitude too and died a hermit, but even alone on Farne he built, dug and sowed."

verdict.reasons:
I re-downloaded the text myself (https://archive.org/download/lifeofsaintphili01bacc/lifeofsaintphili01bacc_djvu.txt). It is byte-identical to the saved bacci1902-v1.txt. It is the Antrobus edition, London, Kegan Paul 1902, vol. 1, which is public domain as a pre-1929 publication. All seven quotations match word for word. Their locations check out: ch. VI on the palpitation of his heart (pp. 23-24); ch. XX "Of Philip's patience" (p. 320); ch. I on his boyhood, "Good Pippo" (pp. 4-5); ch. VII on keeping young people from vice (p. 199); ch. VII on winning souls in his youth (pp. 29-30); ch. VI on his charity for souls (about p. 192).

CHEERFUL HALF: I could not refute it. It is the clearest cheerful temper I have seen checked. Bacci states it as his nature: "a very lively temperament, and without the least tendency to melancholy". He records it from boyhood ("lighthearted... from the kindliness of his temper") to old age ("No one ever saw Philip melancholy... always found him with a cheerful and smiling countenance"). A checker should know one thing. The "temperament" line sits in a sentence about his bodily constitution: Bacci is ruling out that the heart palpitation came from melancholy humours. That is the old humoral sense of temperament, which is exactly Gregory's "by temperament". So it counts, and it is not a guess from a deed.

RESTLESS HALF: recorded, but mixed. For it, as a lifelong habit: "idleness, which he hated so much that no one ever found him unemployed". He "never spared himself in any other kind of toil". He "kept the door of his room always open" and "reserved neither time nor place which he could call his own". When shy visitors held back, "he took him by the hand and drew him in". He walked the squares, shops and banks talking to people. People came "every day" for thirty or forty years. That covers "always doing" and "draws people in" plainly.

AGAINST IT (the candidate's concerns note only the first of these): he "resolved to quit in part the enjoyment of solitude for which he had the greatest attraction". In his hermit years: "Above all things he gave himself to silence, which he prized and practised all his life long, so far as his institute allowed". Even at the Vallicella in 1583 the move "made no difference in his manner of living and his retired habits", and he chose "one of the highest and most remote rooms". At games with the young men he would start play and then retire "to some thicket or hillock" to read or meditate.

So his settled attraction was to quiet, and his busy life was taken on for souls. Note for consistency: the site's Deep Well card puts Gregory the Great on the QUIET side because he "loved the quiet life and had the busy one forced on him". Philip differs in one way. Bacci also records a personal hatred of idleness and a lifelong open door, not just a burden he carried. So Spark is defensible, and most fair readers who know the "Apostle of Rome" would agree. But under the standard this is "one half strongly, the other clearly but not purely", and the card must say so. The fixed text does.

verdict.quoteProblems:
I fetched both texts again from archive.org and checked them. They are saved in scratchpad/skeptic-francis/tc.txt and celano.txt. All eight quotations are word for word, and every section number is right: Three Companions 2 and 4; Celano First Life 2, 56, 71 and 83; Second Life 161. Both translations are public domain under the project's rule: Howell 1908, and 'G. S.' (E. Gurney Salter) 1902, published before 1929. There are three problems, none of them in the quoted words themselves.

(1) 'his attractive disposition was the chief cause that many went after him' is cut off mid-sentence. Celano goes on: 'who were promoters of evil-doing and inciters to crime'. In the source this is a rebuke, not a sign that people caught his energy. Never quote it cut short as praise.

(2) The Morocco line is accurate, but it records one journey driven by a longing for martyrdom ('inebriated in spirit'). That is one deed of zeal, not a temper, so under the standard it cannot carry the restless half.

(3) The draft card's 'he joked in prison' slightly overstates 'even in some sort to jest'. And 'his companions wrote' states an authorship that scholars debate.

'Cheerful countenance' (First Life 83) describes his face and manner in a list of virtues. It supports the cheerful half, but it is not proof on its own.
verdict.reasons:
The cheerful half holds up. The Legend of the Three Companions says his cheerfulness was his nature: 'being by nature joyous and merry' (section 4) and 'a merrier man than was his father' (section 2). His cheerfulness also carries into his adult life. Celano, Second Life 125: 'He strove therefore ever to be gladsome of heart'. First Life 83 gives him a 'cheerful countenance'.

The restless half is strong only for his youth. He went round Assisi 'day and night' with friends, 'given unto jests and songs'. His comrades chose him 'as their master of the revels' (Three Companions 7). Celano, First Life 2: 'He was the admiration of all'.

As an adult the record is genuinely mixed, and the candidate understated the evidence against him. Celano, Second Life 94: 'He always sought out a hidden place'. The same passage: 'If invaded by visits from lay-folk, or by any business, he would cut them short unfinished, and go back to his inward musings'. First Life 103: 'He purposed to fly from intercourse with men'. First Life 71: 'he often used to choose out solitary places'. On the Spark's side, the adult Francis hated idleness (Second Life 161), went round the cities preaching (First Life 36 and 62), and in his last illness his spirit 'became even more active than before' (First Life 97). Second Life 94 directly contradicts the Spark's line 'A quiet week makes you restless' for the grown man.

So include him only with the label 'St Francis of Assisi, as a young man'. That matches the precedent of 'St Augustine, as a young man' and 'St Basil the Great, as a young man'. Repeating the phrase on the same type is a smaller cost than overclaiming. 'In his youth' would work if the owner wants different wording.

A fair reader would accept the young Francis as a Spark, and his popular image (the singing, joyful troubadour) agrees. His youthful spending on feasts also fits the Spark's trap of pleasure, as Augustine's card does.

I rewrote the draft card. It now rests on his youth, drops the Morocco sentence (one deed of zeal), softens the prison joke to match the source, and avoids asserting the debated authorship. It keeps an honest line about his lasting gladness after his conversion, from Second Life 125. There are no pronouns for God in it.

Even then he always tried to stay glad at heart.

verdict.fixedText: A nun who knew him said, “He was always joyous and cheerful, save when moved to compassion by the afflictions of his neighbours.” She also said he spent “the entire day in gaining souls”, preaching and hearing confessions. He walked from town to town, often barefoot. Jordan of Saxony, who knew him, wrote: “By day no one was more accessible and cheerful among his brethren, and by night no one was more watchful in prayer.”
verdict.fixedSrc: Sister Cecilia and Jordan of Saxony, in A. T. Drane, The History of St Dominic
verdict.quoteProblems: None are missing or altered. I downloaded the full text myself (archive.org/download/thehistoryofstdo00cranuoft/thehistoryofstdo00cranuoft_djvu.txt; the metadata gives Drane, Longmans 1891, NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). All six quotations are there word for word, and so is the added phrase "preaching in all the places through which they passed". Page numbers check out: Cecilia is on p. 270, "countenance... kind and joyous" and "as he loved all" are on p. 93, "By day..." is on p. 265, "always made on foot" is on p. 193 and the Segovia grotto is on pp. 284-5. Two small caveats. (1) On p. 93 Drane does not name Jordan as the source of "a countenance that was always kind and joyous". She gives the quote straight after two lines she credits to Jordan ("says the same writer"), and it matches his Libellus. So the attribution is right but only implied on that page. (2) Every line from Cecilia and Jordan is Drane's own 1891 English inside her book, not a separate translation. That is public domain and fine, but the source line should name Drane, as the fixed source line does. I checked one extra line for the fixed text: Cecilia's "It was the constant habit of the venerable Father to spend the entire day in gaining souls, either by continual preaching, or hearing confessions, or in other works of charity" (p. 241). It is verbatim.
verdict.reasons:
CHEERFUL: strong, and recorded as his habit, not as one moment. Several people who knew him say it independently. Sister Cecilia took the habit from him at seventeen, and she describes his appearance: "always joyous and cheerful". Drane reports Rodolph of Faenza's sworn testimony: "always joyous and cheerful". Jordan writes of "a countenance that was always kind and joyous". Drane also mentions "that cheerful and joyous air which was so peculiar to him" and his "simple hearty joyousness". One caveat: Jordan links the cheerful face to inner peace and holiness ("because a joyful heart makes the face cheerful"). But the card for St Antony, already accepted, rests on the same kind of evidence, so the bar is met.

ACTIVE (RESTLESS) HALF: clear in how he lived, but not as a restless temperament, and the sources record strong quiet traits too. For: Cecilia says his "constant habit" was to spend "the entire day in gaining souls". He always travelled on foot, preaching wherever he went. Drane says his life in Rome was "anything but an idle one". Jordan calls him more "accessible and cheerful" than anyone by day and says "as he loved all, so was he beloved by all". That fits "people catch your energy". Against: Drane says that at home or away he "strictly kept the rule of silence" and "was never known to utter an idle word". A woman whose house he often stayed in never heard him speak an idle word. Jordan's rule for him was "the day to our neighbour and the night to God". Solitude "had a singular attraction for him", with night retreats in caves such as Segovia, though that part is partly local tradition. Drane herself sees "a singular mixture" of joyous cheerfulness and "a tender melancholy". Nothing records the Spark's "a quiet week makes you restless". A fair reader would call him cheerful and tirelessly active by day, and quiet and prayerful by night. So "partial" is the honest label.

The candidate's own "partial" rating is correct. The card must show both sides, and the fixed text does by quoting Jordan's whole sentence, night half included.

CHANGES TO THE DRAFT CARD: (1) "A nun... wrote" is now "said". Drane presents Cecilia's account as her narrative ("who says"), and she is known to have dictated it in old age. (2) "His friend Jordan" is now "Jordan of Saxony, who knew him". Jordan was his successor and knew him only briefly, so "friend" overstates it. (3) Jordan's sentence was cut off at "brethren". It is now quoted in full, which shows the balance honestly, so the loose "The nights he gave to God" is dropped. (4) Added Cecilia's first-hand witness to his all-day activity, so the active half rests on a witness and not just on Drane's summary. The sentences are plain and short, with no section numbers. No pronouns for God appear, and "God" is capitalised.

PORTRAIT: confirmed on Wikimedia Commons. The Fra Angelico close-up (San Marco cloister, 1442-45) is 1436x2048, and the smaller Fra_Angelico_St._Dominic.jpg is 301x445. Both are licensed "Public domain". My full-text copy and scripts are in the scratchpad at skeptic-dominic/ (drane.txt, find.py, ctx.py).

# Research brief: the Saints and early Christians hub on wiserwalk.com

## Bottom line
1. **Search demand sits in the long tail, and the pages that rank today are weak there.** Short queries like "st augustine" belong to parishes, schools, a Florida city and Jerome Powell. What a page can win is the informational tail: quotes with a source, feast days in both calendars, "is X a saint in the Orthodox Church", "how did X die", character traits, lists of groups, and saints who struggled with a particular sin.
2. **Nobody covers what this site already has.** Rival pages list the Western feast date only or the Orthodox one only. Their quotations mostly carry no source. None of them has an honest personality angle.
3. **Give each person one page at `/saints/<slug>/`.** 301 the 22 `/early-christian/<slug>/` pages there now: they went live on 2026-09-23, so moving them costs almost nothing. Keep `/figure/` as the page for Bible people. Keep `/personality-type/` as it is.
4. **FAQ rich results are gone** (stopped showing on 7 May 2026). ProfilePage and carousel markup do not fit this kind of page. What still pays: Breadcrumb, Image metadata, Article with `about: Person` plus `sameAs` links to Wikipedia and Wikidata, and a short answer block near the top of each page.
5. **Name:** "Saints" in the menu. "Saints and early Christians" as the hub's heading. Every person who is not counted a saint gets a status line on their card and page.

## 1. What people search, grouped by intent
Sources: Google and Bing autocomplete for 381 seed queries, plus Wikipedia pageviews for the last 12 months (Sep 2025 to Aug 2026). Pageviews are a rough guide to demand, not search volumes.

| Intent | Evidence (autocomplete) | A page per saint answers it? |
|---|---|---|
| Who they were, facts, character | "st benedict character traits and virtues", "st augustine personality type", "st jerome bad temper", "what is st john chrysostom best known for", "who was st patrick really" | Yes. Headline section |
| Death | "how did polycarp die" (8 Bing variants), "ignatius of antioch cause of death", "how old was saint augustine when he died" | Yes. Quick facts plus a short section |
| Feast day, both calendars | "st augustine feast day orthodox", "john chrysostom feast day orthodox" and "…catholic", "st martin of tours orthodox feast day" | Yes. Quick facts |
| Status, East and West | "is augustine a saint in the orthodox church" (10 variants), "is origen a saint (catholic/orthodox/coptic)", "why is tertullian not a saint", "why was clement of alexandria removed as a saint", "is boethius a saint" | Yes. "Is he a saint?" section. This is the site's best edge |
| Quotes | "\<name\> quotes" for nearly every name, "augustine quotes on grace/predestination/free will", "restless heart augustine quote source/context" | Yes, with a source for every line |
| Writings | "\<name\> books/writings/pdf", "rule of st benedict summary", "best church fathers to read first" | Yes. "What to read first" with free links |
| Pronunciation | Augustine of Hippo, Chrysostom, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Boethius, Lactantius, Tertullian, Cyprian | Yes. One line in quick facts (cheap to win) |
| Nicknames and titles | "why was st john chrysostom called golden mouth", "athanasius contra mundum meaning" | Yes. Small facts |
| Relationships | "augustine and monica/ambrose/jerome", "basil and gregory friendship", "were basil the great and gregory of nyssa brothers" | Yes. The existing `pairs` data covers this |
| Controversies | "john chrysostom against the jews", "gregory of nyssa universalism", "st jerome quotes on women", "augustine of hippo ethnicity", "was anthony the great black" | Yes. Plainly, with sources |
| Images | "\<name\> icon" on most Eastern names | Yes. Portraits carrying Image metadata |
| Group lists | "early church fathers list in order/chronological", "list of desert fathers and mothers", "who were the three cappadocian fathers", "apostolic fathers names", "four great doctors of the latin/eastern church", "early christian martyrs list", "early christian women saints", "early church fathers timeline" | No. Group pages |
| Quizzes and personality | "which saint are you quiz" (+ catholic/female/orthodox), "which church father are you quiz", "saint personality test", "saint temperament quiz", "melancholic/choleric/sanguine/phlegmatic saints", "saints mbti" | Partly. Quiz, type and group pages |
| Struggles and temperament lists | "saints who struggled with anger/pride/lust/anxiety/depression", "saints who were introverts/quiet/shy", "saints known for patience/humility" | No. Group pages |
| Quotes by topic | "saint quotes about gratitude/patience/humility/joy/worry/forgiveness/anger/silence" | No. Topic pages cross-linked to the 11 articles |
| Fun formats | "saint trading cards (printable/template/project)", "catholic saint baseball cards", "church fathers tier list" | Yes, as a printable saint card. No tier lists |
| Not ours | "saint of the day", "feast day today", "saints born on \<date\>", "st X church/school", "st benedict medal", "novena", picking a confirmation saint | Skip. Saint-of-the-day is already on the kill list |

**Put the searched name in titles, not the short one.** Each short form below is taken by something else:
- "st augustine" means the Florida city.
- "jerome" means Jerome Powell.
- "st ambrose" means the university.
- "origen" means Orijen dog food.
- "basil the great" means the Disney film The Great Mouse Detective.
- "st cyprian" means Cyprian of Antioch and his "prayer against witchcraft".
- Google turns "antony the great" into "anthony the great". Use "Antony (Anthony) the Great".

**Timely hook:** a feature film, *Moses the Black*, came out on 30 January 2026 and on digital on 13 March ([Deadline](https://deadline.com/2026/02/moses-the-black-omar-epps-wiz-khalifa-quavo-release-dates-1236737100/)). Autocomplete shows "st moses the black story", "…quotes" and "…cause of death". His Wikipedia page drew 145,520 views in 12 months.

## 2. Who ranks today, and where they are weak
- **Life stories:** Wikipedia, Britannica, EWTN, [Catholic Online](https://www.catholic.org/saints/saint.php?saint_id=418), [Franciscan Media](https://www.franciscanmedia.org/saint-of-the-day/saint-augustine-of-hippo/), [Hallow](https://hallow.com/saints/augustine-of-hippo/), mycatholic.life, OrthodoxWiki, [OCA lives](https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2026/11/13/103270-st-john-chrysostom-the-archbishop-of-constantinople).
  - Catholic Online's Augustine page runs about 380 words. Its two quotations have no source. It gives 28 August only and carries about 8 donation or shop prompts, including a modal popup.
  - Franciscan Media runs about 350 words, with no source for Augustine's own words and 28 August only.
  - Hallow is the strongest template: about 1,100 words, a quick-facts box and sourced quotes. It is Catholic only, has no Orthodox date and pushes its app twice.
  - OCA's Chrysostom page is about 2,100 words of narrative. It gives 13 November only, not the Catholic 13 September, and its quotations have no sources.
  - New Advent's Catholic Encyclopedia articles date from 1907 to 1914.
- **Quotes:** Goodreads, AZQuotes, BrainyQuote, QuoteFancy, and listicles from Aleteia, Catholic-Link and EpicPew. Goodreads' most-liked Augustine quote (8,514 likes), "The world is a book…", is misattributed. [Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2025/09/25/world-book/) traces it to Richard Lassels in 1670. Of Goodreads' top 12 Augustine quotes, only 3 name a work. The list also includes lines usually credited to Oscar Wilde ("no saint without a past") and Bernard of Clairvaux ("the measure of love…"). A section called "Often misquoted", with the real source, is original value and easy to share.
- **"Which saint are you":** Loyola Press, BrainFall, CMMB, the Diocese of Westminster, quotev and quizony. [saintdiscoveryquiz.com](https://www.saintdiscoveryquiz.com/) is the closest model: 21 questions, 6 traits, 480+ saint pages. It is Catholic only.
- **"Which church father are you":** First Things and Mike Aquilina's blog (a quiz from 2007), plus Sporcle. Old and thin.
- **Temperament lists:** Catholic Company, CatholicMatch ("Famous Melancholics"), spiritualdirection.com and TAN. They assign modern temperament labels with no source.
- **Anger, introverts and similar:** Aleteia, EWTN GB/ChurchPOP, Catholic Exchange, Busted Halo and blogs. These are listicles with no sources, mostly about modern saints.
- **Group lists:** Wikipedia, Britannica, GotQuestions, catholic.com, CCEL, churchfathers.org, TheCollector, and [theeasternchurch.com](https://www.theeasternchurch.com/saints/desert-fathers-and-mothers) (a 6,500-word guide, Orthodox and Eastern Catholic only).
- **Orthodox status of Augustine:** GOARCH, OrthodoxWiki, OCA Q&A, a Georgetown page and a Substack. Each is a single-tradition voice.

**Gaps the site can fill:**
- Both calendars on one page.
- A work and chapter for every line, plus a list of misattributions.
- A short answer, then scannable blocks, on a phone-first layout with no ads.
- Personality in the saints' own words, tied to the quizzes.
- A sober answer to "is X a saint?"

## 3. What a winning page per saint needs
- **Title** (65 characters or fewer, the searched form of the name plus the most-searched hook). Examples:
  - "Augustine of Hippo: life, personality, quotes and feast days" (58)
  - "St Jerome: temper, translation, quotes and feast day"
  - "Origen of Alexandria: why he is not a saint, and what he taught"
  Vary the hook per person. Do not use one fixed template.
- **Description** (50 to 160 characters, ending with a full stop). Example: "Who Augustine was in plain words: his life, how he died, feast days East and West, his temperament, and quotes with the book and chapter."
- **H1:** the plain name.
- **Near the top:** a "Who was Augustine?" answer of 40 to 60 words. Extend the "In short" check in `seo-test.mjs` (30 to 70 words) to `/saints/*`.
- **Quick-facts card:** born; died and how; where; known for; also called (the Eastern and Western names, e.g. Gregory the Theologian = Gregory Nazianzen); feast days for Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican/Lutheran where they keep one; Old Calendar note (+13 days); status in each church; patron of (only with a source); how to say the name; place in the Personality Test (labelled as our reading); portrait credit.
- **H2s, in plain words:**
  1. What was he like? (character traits in his own words and his friends')
  2. His life in N moments
  3. In his own words (6 to 12 quotes: work, book and chapter, translation, link to a free text)
  4. Often misquoted

  - Boethius has a local cult in Pavia, approved in 1883, feast 23 October.
  - Some Orthodox usage calls Augustine "Blessed".
  - Moses and the prophets are in Orthodox and Catholic calendars; Protestants do not call them saints.
- **Recommendation:**
  - Menu item: "Saints". It fits the tight phone row.
  - Hub H1 "Saints and early Christians"; title "Saints and Church Fathers: lives, quotes, feast days", which covers both main search terms. Pick one visible hub name for the owner to approve.

  - URL `/saints/` for everyone. Readers see the labels, not the path, and one namespace for people beats splitting by a status that differs from church to church.
- **Menu:** rename "Articles" to "Learn" (5 letters instead of 8, which helps the tight row noted in kit.css at line 911). ## 6. Guardrails
- **Calendars:** always print both calendars, with the Old Calendar +13 days note. Check each date against the General Roman Calendar, OCA/GOARCH calendars, LSB/ELW (Lutheran) and Lesser Feasts and Fasts (Episcopal). Examples:
  - Martin: 11 November (West), 12 November (East).
  - Chrysostom: 13 September (Catholic); 13 November, 27 January and 30 January (Orthodox).
  - Basil and Gregory: 2 January (Catholic); 1 January, 25 January and 30 January (Orthodox).
  - Augustine: 28 August (West), 15 June (Orthodox).
- **Names and "St":** H1s and URLs use plain names. A "Called" line gives each church's title. Never write "St" for Tertullian, Origen or Lactantius. Bible people are "honoured as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic calendars", never simply "St Moses".
- **Quotes:** a work, section and translation for every line. Verify them by script against the public-domain source, the same way `verify.mjs` and quiz #4's VERIFY.md do. Compare case-insensitively, because of the owner's capitals rule for God. Misattributions go in their own list, with evidence.
- **Hard topics:** state them, in both the holders' and the critics' words (Adversus Judaeos, universalism, Jerome on women, Tertullian's Montanism). Hiding them fails a discernment audience.
- **"Stat sheets":** only facts with a source (dates, places, number of surviving works with a source, titles) plus the site's quiz placements, labelled as ours. No invented ratings. No tier lists. The printable saint card is where the playfulness goes.
- **Prayers:** no intercession prayers or novenas. Count knowledge, never devotion. A prayer the saint actually wrote is fine.
- **Writing:** plain short sentences, no filler, no section marks, say a thing once.
